title: The thing about AI game dev, is that it feels more like being a director, rather than a programmer.
author: ForgotMyAcc
selftext: I can mark, draw and ramble into my mic - and send it off. I haven't touched lines of code except for .env's and quickly adjusting variables for quite a while now! Anyone else in a similar situation feeling good?

comments.author: Own_Principle_7901
comments.body: It warms my heart seeing people being critical and constructive when requesting changes. It proves the dev cares about the results and tests it at each iteration to improve. It should be the norm, but it seems so hare based on the unpolished and unbalanced garbage being spilled everyday.

replies.author: ForgotMyAcc
replies.body:
Definitely. I think the influx of people who’ve never made software are often so amazed it works that they don’t ask how, why, or who it’s for- that'll come with experience.

Every design choice and game mechanic should go through multiple passes. Good software takes iteration, and plenty of “kill your darlings.”, AI or not.

replies.author: Niket_N1ghtWing
replies.body: I am surprised you are getting downvoted for stating the obvious. It used to be hard and now it is easier to do but the tools have been there for a long time. Being an amazing coder was never really a strict requirement to build games in most cases before either. UE, Unity, Godot have always been literally free to use and they already gave you the ability to build products without understanding much about the engine itself. Now Ai has given us the ability to build products that we dont understand much about.

replies.author: Spudly42
replies.body: Worth noting that a lot of people using AI in game dev have been doing the game dev thing for 5, 10, 15+ years, so we know about most all of the tools and how best to leverage them.  In those cases, the same tools get used, but with AI there is so much more time and opportunity to refine, polish, fix bugs, improve performance and make deeper games.

comments.author: NeusomaDev
comments.body:
I've baked my own QA testing into each loop of production so that I make sure things work as intended, and Claude designed its own sets of headless tests so that I'm never handed something completely hot off the presses. I hardly even look at code, although there's a shitload of natural language spec that goes into the briefing process. So yes, we're directors at this point, not programmers. I started jokingly calling myself a "creative director" to annoy my friends and while that still feels pretentious AF, the concept is at least not a joke anymore (even if the gravitas of the title still feels massively unearned until I ship something, lol...).

Digging the texture of the background btw! Cute art style.

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
I don't agree. I have done managerial work before, and it always felt basically awful. 

  
This is more like... I dunno what it's like. It's the satisfaction of just writing out a design document, while brainstorming at the same time, and then a fckn magical genie starts turning that brainstorming and technical document into a prototype in realtime that can be easily bootstrapped into a fully functional game module. 

I cannot think of a single thing this is remotely like. I have total agency, so it's not like being part of a team or collaboration; I don't have the headaches or guilt of managerial authority; I'm not spending time doing one process and then shifting gears to another - it's all very fluid and holistic; I'm neither aiming for nor waiting for an approaching deadline... 

  
The closest thing, honestly, is fckn therapy. It feels like the same process, only instead of a therapist helping me sort my shit out, it's a machine converting my shit into tangible reality (just to be clear, I am not equating the machine with actual therapy; you should NOT be using the machine as a fckn therapist, like, obviously not - just the overall cadence and vibe of the experience, where one party vents their shit out and the other party turns that exhaust into something useful).

comments.author: elliuotatar
comments.body:
The thing about AI game development is I'm on a Pro subscription with Google and last night I decided to chat a bit with Argon about a potential game concept and how to have it implement it, and after about ten responses from it where I'd barely begun just hashing out the story, it told me I'd been using it too much and I'd have to wait an hour for it to refresh. 

Now maybe that was my bad for using their newest model, but that's just ridiculous. I'm paying for this shit and they don't show me how much of my compute each model will use. With Flow they tell me that different operations will take different amounts of credits.

comments.author: arcane_words
comments.body: This is exactly what I have been doing.  I am a decent programmer (do it for a living and all) but I haven't touched the code.  I consider myself the manager, and Claude my team.  I give instructions and make decisions.  Usually I have Claude write the spec, I clear up any mistakes, and claude writes the implementation guide.  Whenever I have tokens, I send Claude off to implement another chunk.
